"2.3 Measures and Sanctions In 2024, the BaFin initiated a total of 195 fine proceedings. It imposed fines amounting to a total of 39,860,350 euros.6

To protect the stability, functionality, and integrity of the German financial system and the collective interests of consumers, the BaFin can take various actions. It engages in dialogue with supervised companies, can raise issues verbally or in writing, and demand that the affected companies rectify any problems. However, it can also take measures and impose sanctions. This strengthens the collective protection of investors and the integrity of the financial market, as the publication of its actions also has a general preventive effect.

Measures
The BaFin can take supervisory measures that are laid down in various sector-specific laws. With administrative acts that impose a burden, the BaFin can proceed against legal entities as well as natural persons, but also against unknown parties. Measures are intended to have a preventive effect: their goal is to avert dangers. Therefore, a measure does not necessarily have to be preceded by a legal violation.

Supervisory measures include, for example, special audits, capital add-ons, business restrictions, transaction bans, license withdrawals, or the appointment of special representatives in the affected companies. They are supposed to oversee the implementation of measures in the affected companies.

The BaFin can also appoint special representatives with the authority of a managing director. They then partially or completely take over the tasks of a managing director or an organ of the affected company.

The legal basis for this is regulated, among other things, by the Banking Act (KWG), the Capital Investment Code (KAGB), the Insurance Supervision Act (VAG), the Payment Services Supervision Act (ZAG), or the Money Laundering Act (GWG).

Sanctions: Nearly 40 Million Euros in Fines
In addition, the BaFin can penalize legal violations – with fines. For this purpose, it initiates proceedings according to the Act on Administrative Offences (OWiG). Fines are sanctions. Unlike measures, they initially have a repressive effect. However, they are also intended to encourage the perpetrators to comply with the legal requirements in the future.
6 See Chapter I.2.4.3 Consumer-protective conduct and market supervision.
Annual Report 2024 I Highlights | 22

2.3.1 Credit Institutions, Payment and E-Money Institutions, Leasing and Factoring Institutions, Crypto Custodians, Crypto Securities Registry Operators, and Credit Service Providers under the Secondary Credit Market Act
In 2024, the BaFin issued 768 measures in the banking sector (see Table 9, page 23). In 2023, the number of complaints and measures had returned to the level before the Covid-19 pandemic.

In 2024, the BaFin appointed nine special representatives in banking supervision (previous year: six).

2.3.2 Insurance Companies and Pension Funds
In 2024, the BaFin also identified significant deficiencies in IT audits at insurance companies. In the case of one insurance company, due to violations of the requirements for proper business organization within the meaning of the VAG, it imposed a capital add-on to the solvency capital requirement. The company must rectify the deficiencies within a deadline set by the BaFin. The measure is intended to ensure compliance within a specified period."

2.3.7 Integrity of the Financial System
2.3.7.1 Licensing Requirement
Anyone who wishes to conduct banking, investment, insurance, or e-money business, or provide financial, credit, crowdfunding services, or payment services in Germany generally requires written permission from BaFin. Once BaFin has granted permission, the provider is under its ongoing supervision. In 2024, BaFin received 833 requests for permission (previous year: 841). As in the previous year, a large part of these concerned payment services and crypto-based business models.

For young companies in the financial sector, it is crucial to know whether their planned activity requires permission from BaFin. To facilitate low-threshold interaction with the supervisory authority, BaFin developed the new format of the Pop-up Embassy. Here, experts from different areas of BaFin answer technical questions from FinTechs on-site. In 2024, the Pop-up Embassy took place during the FinTech fair FIBE in Berlin and at the TechQuartier in Frankfurt am Main.

Exemption from Licensing Requirement and Ongoing Supervision
Under strict conditions and only upon application, BaFin can exempt a company from the licensing requirement for a materially limited business (§ 2 paragraph 4 KWG). This is only possible as long as the institution does not require supervision according to BaFin's assessment of the nature of its business. In 2024, this concerned 154 institutions (previous year: 163 institutions).

Companies from a third country can also be exempted by BaFin: According to § 2 paragraph 5 KWG, this is possible if the company is subject to equivalent supervision in its home country. This makes additional supervision by BaFin unnecessary. Such exemptions exist for institutions from the USA, Canada, Australia, Switzerland, and Singapore. In 2024, 114 institutions were exempted under § 2 paragraph 5 KWG (previous year: 115 institutions).

2.3.7.2 Prosecution of Unauthorized Business
Anyone who operates a business requiring permission without authorization endangers the integrity of the financial system and commits a criminal offense. Therefore, BaFin must pursue violations of the licensing requirement.

2.3.6 Anti-Money Laundering Prevention
In 2024, BaFin again identified deficiencies in anti-money laundering prevention at institutions and consequently issued measures against these institutions. As a result of sustained violations of the Money Laundering Act (GwG), several measures were taken against executive directors. The executive directors bear the responsibility for proper business organization, which includes measures to prevent money laundering and terrorist financing.

To promote the timely and sustainable rectification of deficiencies, BaFin issued several orders. These also include the imposition of coercive fines for inadequate or untimely remediation of deficiencies. Furthermore, BaFin commissioned auditing firms as special representatives to monitor and report on the elimination of deficiencies in institutions. At the end of 2024, special representatives were active in seven institutions (previous year: seven). Of these, special representatives were newly appointed in three institutions in 2024 (previous year: three). The institutions affected were very diverse, with profound structural deficiencies. Three newly appointed special representatives were equipped with executive powers to promote the elimination of the deficiencies. In three institutions, the appointments expired in 2024.

The BaFin published the compact information Finance.Information.Tips., which according to DORA must be mandatorily agreed upon between the financial company and the ICT third-party service provider.
Key topics were digital financial transactions, fraud schemes in the financial market, and investment. BaFin also informed consumers in webinars and at trade fairs. For example, in October 2024, it was represented with an information booth at the "With Money and Understanding" financial education festival in Berlin.

2.5 Digitalization

2.5.1 DORA

Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience in the financial sector (Digital Operational Resilience Act – DORA) is intended to make the European financial sector more resilient to cyber-attacks and risks from information and communication technology (ICT). DORA affects all financial sectors. The regulation came into force on January 17, 2023, and will be applied from January 17, 2025. Since then, DORA has been the basis for supervision in the field of IT/cybersecurity.

In Germany alone, DORA affects an estimated more than 3,600 financial sector companies, most of which are already supervised by BaFin. However, ICT third-party service providers are also increasingly coming into the focus of supervision with DORA. For ICT third-party service providers critical to the European financial sector, DORA creates a European supervisory framework involving national supervisory authorities – including BaFin. BaFin has intensively prepared for its new tasks that will arise with DORA in 2024. Since mid-2024, BaFin has provided an overview of the contractual contents published, which must be mandatorily agreed upon according to DORA between the financial company and the ICT third-party service provider.

In 2024, the EU Commission issued numerous technical regulatory and implementation standards (RTS or ITS) that specify DORA. In addition, the German legislator has taken steps to implement DORA at the national level with the Financial Market Digitalization Act.

BaFin has been intensively involved in shaping the regulations around DORA. For this purpose, it has collaborated on the drafts of Level-2 and Level-3 texts (RTS, ITS, Guidelines) in the European supervisory authorities. To prepare for DORA, BaFin has implemented various projects. For example, it has provided technical solutions for the reporting requirements demanded under DORA and the adjustment of internal audit guidelines for supervisory IT audits. In mid-2024, BaFin published an overview of the contractual contents that are mandatory to agree upon according to DORA between the financial company and the ICT third-party service provider.

BaFin provides comprehensive information

On its website, BaFin has already set up a separate section on the topic of DORA in 2023. This has been continuously expanded and updated in 2024 to inform affected companies about the current state of regulation and to address industry questions in FAQs. In addition, numerous specialist articles and background interviews on DORA have appeared on BaFin's website. At its cross-sectoral conference "IT Supervision in the Financial Sector" in September 2024, BaFin informed more than 1,000 participants about the EU regulation and was also available to answer questions.

2.5.2 MiCAR

Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 on markets in crypto-assets (Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation – MiCAR) came into force on June 29, 2023. It creates a harmonized European regulatory framework for crypto-assets. The goal: to safeguard financial stability and investor protection, to promote innovation, and to enable the potential of crypto-assets to be fully exploited.

Since December 30, 2024, MiCAR has been fully applicable. Since then, BaFin has been responsible for supervising issuers of asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens as well as crypto-asset service providers.

BaFin has informed extensively

Since mid-2024, BaFin has published extensive information on MiCAR on its website. There, one can find a roadmap for different categories of applicants and institutions, supervisory requirements for institutions providing crypto-asset services, as well as a FAQ list. The information is continuously updated.

The national regulations that flank MiCAR can be found in the Financial Market Digitalization Act.

2.5.3 Automated Data Analysis

The "New Internal Model QRTs" project group of the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) has developed an interactive app. The app is designed to support data-based supervision over internal models.
